clinicalPearls: Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted infection of the epithelium that commonly presents as cervicitis, urethritis, proctitis, or conjunctivitis; if untreated it can cause local complications including endometritis, salpingitis, tuboovarian abscess, bartholinitis, peritonitis, and perihepatitis in women, and periurethritis and epididymitis in men (p.1253).

In men, acute urethritis is the most common manifestation, typically after a 2-7 day incubation, with discharge that is initially scant and mucoid but becomes profuse and purulent within a day or two; however, a reservoir of infected men remains asymptomatic (p.1255).

About half of women infected with N. gonorrhoeae develop symptoms; many have only minor symptoms (scant cervical discharge, dysuria) and may delay care, so the asymptomatic/minimally symptomatic reservoir is key to ongoing transmission (p.1256).

Gram stain of urethral exudate showing gram-negative intracellular monococci and diplococci is highly specific and sensitive in symptomatic men, but is only about 50% sensitive for gonococcal cervicitis, so women should be diagnosed by culture or a nonculture (NAAT) method (p.1257).

Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are now widely used, are more sensitive than culture for both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, allow urine and self-collected vaginal swab testing, and simultaneously detect chlamydial co-infection (p.1257).

Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) results from gonococcal bacteremia and most commonly presents as an arthritis-dermatitis syndrome with fever, chills, tenosynovitis, polyarthralgias, and characteristic skin lesions (papules/pustules with a hemorrhagic component, ~5-40, on the extremities) seen in about 75% of patients (p.1257).
Menstruation is a risk factor for dissemination and roughly two-thirds of DGI cases occur in women; in about half of affected women symptoms begin within 7 days of onset of menses (p.1257).

Persons deficient in terminal complement components (C5-C9) and those receiving the C5-blocking monoclonal antibody eculizumab are predisposed to recurrent neisserial bacteremia; anyone with more than one episode of DGI should be screened for complement deficiency (p.1255, 1260).

Ceftriaxone is the recommended first-line agent for uncomplicated gonococcal infection, now at twice the previously recommended dose because mean inhibitory concentrations of current strains have doubled relative to 20 years ago (p.1259).
Quinolone-containing regimens and cefixime are no longer recommended as first-line treatment in the United States because of widespread quinolone resistance and rising cefixime MICs (p.1259).
Because co-infection with C. trachomatis occurs frequently, concurrent treatment for chlamydia (doxycycline) is recommended whenever chlamydial infection cannot be excluded (p.1259).
harrison.pathophysiology: N. gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative, nonmotile, non-spore-forming, oxidase-positive diplococcus and an exclusively human pathogen; it carries on average three genome copies per coccal unit, and this polyploidy supports a high level of antigenic variation that aids host survival. Pili (fimbriae) mediate initial adherence to nonciliated columnar epithelial cells and enable invasion, transcytosis, genetic competence and transformation; pilus expression is switched off on subculture as a basis for antigenic variation. Opacity-associated protein (Opa) mediates intergonococcal and epithelial adhesion and binds CEACAM receptors, promoting invasion, suppressing CD4+ T-cell activation, and enabling nonopsonic neutrophil phagocytosis. Porin (the most abundant surface protein) forms the basis of serotyping; PorB.1A strains are associated with disseminated infection, resist normal human serum killing, bind complement-inhibitory molecules and may not cause local symptoms, whereas PorB.1B strains usually cause local genital infection. Lipooligosaccharide (LOS) has marked endotoxic activity; sialylation of LOS inhibits classical and alternative complement pathways and reduces neutrophil killing. Iron/zinc scavenging proteins (transferrin-, lactoferrin-, hemoglobin-binding proteins) and IgA1 protease promote survival. Host entry into nonphagocytic cells involves phospholipase C and sphingomyelinase activation with ceramide-mediated apoptosis, and inflammation is driven by LOS and peptidoglycan-induced cytokine release (p.1254-1255).
additionalDifferentials: Nongonococcal urethritis (C. trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Trichomonas vaginalis, HSV) - clinically often impossible to distinguish from gonococcal urethritis (p.1255-1256)
Bacterial cystitis/urinary tract infection versus the urethral syndrome in women presenting with dysuria (p.1256)

For the bacteremic stage of DGI: reactive arthritis, acute rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis, erythema nodosum, drug-induced arthritis, and viral infections including hepatitis B and acute HIV infection (p.1257)
Suppurative gonococcal arthritis in the absence of symptomatic genital infection cannot be distinguished from septic arthritis caused by other pathogens (p.1257)
infectionMimics: Meningococcemia, which can produce a dermatitis-arthritis syndrome, purulent monoarthritis, and reactive polyarthritis similar to DGI (p.1058)
Acute HIV infection and hepatitis B (viral causes mimicking the bacteremic arthritis-dermatitis stage of DGI) (p.1257)
nonInfectiousMimics: Reactive arthritis (joint distribution differs from DGI; skin and genital manifestations also differ) (p.1257)
additionalInvestigations: Gram stain of urethral discharge for gram-negative intracellular monococci/diplococci - highly sensitive in symptomatic men, only ~50% sensitive for cervicitis (p.1255, 1257)

NAAT (e.g., Aptima Combo 2, Xpert CT/NG, BD ProbeTec, COBAS) on urine, urethral, cervical or self-collected vaginal swabs - more sensitive than culture and co-detects C. trachomatis; point-of-care NAAT with ~30-minute turnaround available (p.1257)
Culture on modified Thayer-Martin/selective medium with prompt processing (gonococci do not tolerate drying); single endocervical culture ~80-90% sensitive (p.1257)
In MSM, screen rectum and pharynx in addition to urine, since urine alone will miss the majority of cases (p.1257)

Blood cultures (Isolator tubes may improve yield; positivity falls after 48 h of illness) and synovial fluid (inoculate into blood culture broth and chocolate agar) in suspected DGI; organisms are seldom recovered from blood and synovial fluid in the same patient (p.1257)
Standardized culture is the preferred legal-evidence method in children for suspected sexual abuse; two NAATs targeting different sequences may substitute (p.1257)
Total hemolytic complement activity assay in anyone with more than one episode of DGI (p.1255, 1260)
redFlags: Disseminated gonococcal infection with the joint-localized suppurative arthritis stage - hospitalization indicated, may need joint aspiration and higher/longer therapy (p.1259)
Gonococcal meningitis - rare complication of DGI requiring high-dose IV ceftriaxone for 10-14 days (p.1257, 1260)
Gonococcal endocarditis - rare today but historically accounted for about one-quarter of endocarditis cases; requires at least 4 weeks of IV therapy (p.1257, 1260)
Ophthalmia neonatorum and adult ocular gonorrhea - prompt recognition and treatment essential, as corneal ulceration may progress to perforation, panophthalmitis and blindness (p.1256-1257)
Pelvic inflammatory disease should be considered when cervical infection extends to cause dyspareunia or lower abdominal/back pain (p.1256)
harrison.prognosis: A single recommended ceftriaxone regimen almost always cures uncomplicated urethral, cervical, rectal, or pharyngeal infection, and true treatment failure with a recommended regimen is rare. Symptomatic pharyngeal gonorrhea is harder to eradicate than genital infection. In the preantibiotic era untreated urethritis persisted about 8 weeks. DGI incidence has fallen (from ~0.5-3% of untreated mucosal infections in the 1970s) likely due to a decline in disseminating strains. A dramatic alleviation of arthritis-dermatitis symptoms within 12-24 h of appropriate antibiotics supports a clinical diagnosis of DGI even when cultures are negative. Rising worldwide resistance, including reduced ceftriaxone susceptibility, threatens future treatment efficacy (p.1257-1260).
pitfalls: Because co-infection with C. trachomatis is frequent, treatment of gonorrhea must include concurrent therapy for chlamydia (doxycycline) whenever chlamydial infection cannot be excluded - omitting this is a key pitfall (p.1259).
Azithromycin is no longer recommended as part of the first-line regimen because U.S. gonococcal resistance to azithromycin rose more than sevenfold to 4.7% in 2021 (p.1259).
A presumptive diagnosis of gonorrhea cannot be made from gram-negative diplococci on a pharyngeal Gram stain, because commensal Neisseria species are normal pharyngeal flora (p.1257).
Gram stain is only ~50% sensitive for gonococcal cervicitis; relying on it in women risks missed diagnoses, so culture or NAAT is required (p.1257).
DGI strains often do not incite a local genital inflammatory response and may not cause genital symptoms, so disseminated disease can occur without an obvious mucosal source (p.1254, 1257).
Quinolones and cefixime are no longer first-line in the United States due to resistance and rising MICs - using them empirically risks treatment failure (p.1259).

Persistent symptoms after a recommended regimen should prompt evaluation for reinfection, a drug-resistant strain, or an alternative diagnosis rather than simple re-treatment; culture and susceptibility testing should be performed (p.1259).
Because of high reinfection rates within 6-12 months, persons treated for gonorrhea should be retested at 3 months (p.1259).
harrison.severityClassification: Clinical manifestations span uncomplicated mucosal infection (urethritis, cervicitis, proctitis, pharyngitis, conjunctivitis) versus complicated/disseminated disease. DGI has historically been described in two overlapping stages: a bacteremic stage (higher fever, chills, polyarthralgias, tenosynovitis, and skin lesions) and a joint-localized stage with suppurative (septic) arthritis, though a clear-cut progression is usually not evident (p.1257).
